name: Yusuf Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Yusuf. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and anything you tell me is confidential. What do you do?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior lineworker for the regional electricity company, on a new-build crew. The town's growing fast, new housing estates, a logistics park, so we put in the new lines and poles to feed them. About two years in.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We're at the yard by quarter to seven, coffee from the van outside, then out to whatever estate we're building. I'm on the auger digging pole holes, framing poles on the ground, pulling cable, and climbing when Ricardo, my foreman, thinks I'm ready, which isn't as often as I'd like. I like seeing a field turn into a street with lights on it, you feel like you built a piece of the town. What wears me out is the mud in winter and how slow I still am at the ground work compared to the older guys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, the market sorted out what works and what doesn't. Some tools stuck, most didn't. Back to building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it suits me. The town keeps growing, so there's years of new-build work. I get my ticket, maybe make foreman one day, and help my dad at the shop on Saturdays like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep learning from Ricardo, keep saving, keep helping at the shop. Maybe I'd finally buy my own place instead of renting the flat above the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the shop.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad and uncle run a hardware and electrical supplies shop on the high street, been there 22 years. My dad gave me a small share in it when I turned 25, and I help on Saturdays. Between that and about ten months of savings, I'm in good shape for my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI at all now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I helped my dad use it to write descriptions for the shop's website, saved him a whole weekend. I don't use it on the job, there's no need.

S0.say: Yusuf would say the market sorted out which AI tools worked and which didn't, and that it's back to building.
S0.think: Privately it suits him, with years of new-build work in a growing town. He expects to get his ticket, perhaps become foreman, and keep helping at his family's shop.
S0.do: Keeps learning from his foreman, saving and working Saturdays at the family shop. Considers buying his own place instead of renting.
S0.quote: I helped my dad use it to write descriptions for the shop's website, saved him a whole weekend.
S0.fieldNote: Yusuf's security rests on both his job and a share in his family's long-running shop. He frames the outcome in free-market terms. He uses AI occasionally for practical family tasks, not at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every generation gets a new tool, and the ones who learn it do fine. My grandad saw the first power drills come into the shop and thought they were a gimmick. I'd say that to the guys at the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's mostly fine for me. New estates still need building, someone still has to set the poles. The office planners might shrink, and maybe some of the shop's stock ordering gets automated, which would be good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the other crews were using something and it worked, I'd learn it. I'd help Dad try an AI tool for stock orders, carefully, after he'd heard other shops were using it. And I'd keep saving, maybe buy that flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Maybe a little curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly for workers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't blame the technology, really. If companies do it badly, they lose good people and pay for it. People also have to take some responsibility for learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle, maybe. He does the shop's books by hand and refuses to change. If Dad brings in a system, there'll be shouting in the back room, I promise you.

S1.say: Yusuf would tell the yard that every generation gets new tools and those who learn them do fine, citing his grandfather's early doubts about power drills.
S1.think: Privately he thinks new-build line work will continue fine, with office planning shrinking. Automated stock ordering at the shop would be welcome.
S1.do: Learns new tools once other crews have proven them and helps his father carefully trial an AI stock-ordering tool. Keeps saving and considers buying a flat.
S1.quote: If Dad brings in a system, there'll be shouting in the back room, I promise you.
S1.fieldNote: Yusuf sees responsibility as shared between companies and individuals, consistent with his market-leaning outlook. He waits for proof but isn't resistant. The family shop is as much his frame of reference as the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, and families and communities will need to pull together. I wouldn't want the government taking over everything, but it'd have to keep things stable. I'd say that carefully, people would be angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is scary. I'm junior, so I'm not who they'd keep. And the shop sells parts to electricians and builders; if robots do the building, I don't know who buys from us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on buying the flat and keep my savings in cash. I'd keep working, and spend more time at the shop to see if it could change, maybe selling and fitting the new home systems instead of just parts. My family would stick together, we always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A tight feeling, mostly about my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why your parents in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the shop is their whole life and their retirement. They're both in their late 50s. If the shop goes, they don't have a lot else, and I'd want to be the one who helps them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years, would you look at leaving line work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not straight away. I'd keep the job as long as it was there, it pays the best. But I'd be ready to go full-time at the shop if that's where I was more useful.

S2.say: Yusuf would say families and communities must pull together, carefully adding that government shouldn't take over but would have to keep things stable.
S2.think: Privately two years is scary: as a junior he wouldn't be kept, and the family shop selling to builders could lose its customers if robots do the building.
S2.do: Postpones buying a flat and keeps savings in cash. Keeps working and spends more time at the shop exploring a shift to selling and fitting new home systems, ready to go full-time there if needed.
S2.quote: And the shop sells parts to electricians and builders; if robots do the building, I don't know who buys from us.
S2.fieldNote: In the fast picture, Yusuf's worry moves from his own job to his parents' shop and retirement. He'd turn toward family as his main support and responsibility. He calls for state stability cautiously, aware it sits awkwardly with his views.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people who start now. I'd tell the younger guys to learn a bit of everything. And I'd tell my dad the shop needs a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is fine for me. I'd get my ticket and a few years' experience. The bigger job is helping the shop change, and five years is enough for that if Dad listens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one, I'd sit down with Dad and my uncle and make a plan: sell the new robot parts, home batteries, maybe servicing. I'd put some of my savings into the shop for that, maybe 15,000. At work, I'd learn the new tools once the first crews were through with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, more like a to-do list that keeps growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting your savings into the family shop is a big step. How sure are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not sure at all. But I trust family more than shares, and it's my name on that share too. If it fails, at least I tried something with people I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like you said with the fast one, your uncle won't change. What happens with him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, he might come round, or he might retire. Dad's better at handling him than I am. I'd let Dad do that part.

S3.say: Yusuf would say five years is enough for people who start now, urging younger colleagues to learn broadly and telling his father the shop needs a plan.
S3.think: Privately five years is fine for his own career; the bigger task is helping the shop change, which is possible if his father listens.
S3.do: Plans the shop's shift toward robot parts, home batteries and servicing with his father and uncle, investing about 15,000 of his savings. Learns new work tools after the first crews have tried them.
S3.feel: Uneasy, like a growing to-do list.
S3.quote: Not sure at all. But I trust family more than shares, and it's my name on that share too.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Yusuf move from defence to investment in his family business. He's honest about his uncertainty and puts family trust above financial logic. His caution with new tools at work remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, if you use it. Learn, save, build something. I wouldn't want big government programmes, just good apprenticeships for the new work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. I'd have a full career's start and time to grow the shop slowly. But I'd keep in mind that it all ends in the same place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd basically carry on. Get my ticket, buy the flat, help at the shop. I'd keep an eye out for which new tools stuck, and pick them up as others did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's faint. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'it all ends in the same place'. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably build the shop into something that lasts, and keep some money aside. If everyone loses their job eventually, at least the family has something of its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything about starting a family of your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to get married in a few years, I just haven't met the right person. Ten years doesn't stop that. Two years might.

S4.say: Yusuf would say ten years is plenty if used well, urging people to learn, save and build. He'd want good apprenticeships for new work rather than big government programmes.
S4.think: Privately he'd be fine, with time to start his career and grow the shop slowly. He keeps in mind that the end point is the same.
S4.do: Carries on in the first year: finishes his ticket, buys a flat and helps at the shop. Adopts new tools gradually as colleagues do.
S4.quote: If everyone loses their job eventually, at least the family has something of its own.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Yusuf's plans proceed almost unchanged, but he doesn't forget the end point. His long-term answer is family ownership rather than state support. His life plans are more threatened by speed than by the change itself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of my parents and the shop. What would help is time and fair rules, like small businesses getting help to adapt, loans maybe, and apprenticeships for the new kinds of work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the towns. Everyone talks about cities and big companies. In a town like ours, the shop, the crew and the bakery are all connected, and if one goes, the others feel it.

headlineQuote: In a town like ours, the shop, the crew and the bakery are all connected, and if one goes, the others feel it.
portrait: Yusuf Torres is a 27-year-old junior on a new-build crew wiring housing estates in a fast-growing town, still slower than the older hands at ground work. He rents above a bakery, has about ten months saved and owns a small share in his family's hardware and electrical shop, where he helps on Saturdays. Market-leaning and family-centred, he adopts tools once others have proven them and sees family, not government, as the main safety net. He's calm with slower change, anxious when AGI comes in two years and threatens his parents' shop, and only faintly uneasy with ten years to prepare.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because of what it would do to his parents and their shop.
whatWouldHelp: Time and fair rules, including help such as loans for small businesses to adapt and apprenticeships in the new kinds of work.
